The northern yellow bat (Lasiurus intermedius) exhibits a maximum basal metabolic rate of 18.30 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 18.30 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at the standard body temperature typical of active thermoregulation at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This level of oxygen consumption reflects the moderate energetic demands of a medium-sized vespertilionid, consistent with values reported for other foliage-roosting members of the genus Lasiurus. Field respirometry trials conducted on freshly captured individuals during the summer active season have confirmed this measurement, which aligns closely with predictions based on the species' body mass. The metabolic rate at this core temperature provides a useful baseline for understanding the daily energy budget of this bat during the warm months when it engages in nocturnal foraging and reproductive activities. Comparative data from congeners suggest that the ability to maintain a stable body temperature around 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] during rest is critical for sustaining the physiological processes necessary for flight and lactation. Such measurements are essential for constructing accurate bioenergetic models that can predict how this species might respond to environmental perturbations.

Adult females of this species attain an ultimate wet weight of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams], representing the maximum body mass recorded for reproductively active individuals in the population. This value is derived from extensive field measurements of captured females during the late spring and early summer, when they carry the additional mass associated with pregnancy and fat reserves. The rapid post-natal growth trajectory that follows is fueled by the mother's rich milk production during the lactation period.

Following parturition, the offspring remain dependent on maternal milk for a period estimated at 34 days since birth [tx = 34 days since birth], after which they are weaned and begin to consume solid food at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This weaning age is again based on comparative data from the hoary bat, as direct long-term observations of this solitary, foliage-roosting species are challenging to obtain in the wild. The timing of weaning is a critical life-history transition, marking the point at which the young must achieve nutritional independence and develop the foraging skills necessary to capture flying insects on their own.

Females of Lasiurus intermedius typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with each litter consisting of two to three pups [N_R_i = each litter consisting of two to three pups] born during the early summer months. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species under natural conditions, estimated at 14 years [am = 14 years], highlights a relatively slow pace of life compared to many small mammals, though it is within the range observed for other vespertilionid bats at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C].
